title: A New Toad Species Emerges from the La Brea Tar Pits
gist: A Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology study describes several fossil frog species from the La Brea Tar Pits, including a never-before-described spadefoot toad, because natural bitumen preserves fragile amphibian bodies that normally disintegrate before fossilizing.

insights.claim: Frogs are systematically underrepresented in the fossil record because their soft bodies and fragile bones disintegrate, meaning existing knowledge of ancient amphibian ecology is built on a thin and biased sample.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Any dataset with a known preservation bias understates diversity — expect described amphibian species counts to keep rising as unusual preservation sites are mined.
insights.quote: Frogs don’t preserve well in the fossil record. Their soft bodies and fragile bones are likely to just disintegrate.

insights.claim: Natural asphalt (bitumen) at La Brea worked as both trap and preservative — immobilizing animals and then infusing their bodies — which is why an urban Los Angeles site holds a record concentration of Pleistocene life from about 45,000 years ago onward.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Hydrocarbon seeps are an underexploited high-yield archive; watch for similar tar/asphalt sites being re-surveyed for soft-bodied taxa.
insights.quote: The natural asphalt—crude oil called “bitumen”—acted like a sticky trap, immobilizing animals in the pits and eventually infusing their bodies, preserving 19 species of extinct mammals and 16 extinct birds.

insights.claim: La Brea's asphalt deposits have already yielded 19 species of extinct mammals and 16 extinct birds, a scale of extinct-taxa recovery that anchors the site as a reference collection rather than a curiosity.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Concrete yield numbers justify continued funding and re-analysis of legacy collections at a single site.

insights.claim: The new spadefoot toad species came from re-reviewing fossils already sitting in the tar pit's Hancock Collection, not from new excavation — existing museum backlogs are a live source of first descriptions.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Discovery rate can rise without new fieldwork spend; curation and comparative reference specimens are the binding constraint, not digging.
insights.locator: Headed by lead study author Alberto Cruz

insights.claim: Lead author Alberto Cruz initially read the new toad's distinguishing anatomy as pathology — deformity from illness or injury — and only comparison against modern spadefoot specimens reclassified it as a new species.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A reminder that anomaly-vs-noise calls hinge on having the right comparison set; the same error mode applies to any outlier-detection process.
insights.quote: At first, Cruz thought that the new toad species was deformed from illness or injury, but his comparisons with modern spadefoot toad specimens brought to light its unique features.
